title: Who pays, who owns and who decides: reforming the water sector
label: 20 October 2026 · Reforming the water sector
summary: The Committee examined how privatisation, regulation and finance have shaped England and Wales’ water services since 1989, compared alternative ownership models (public, mutual, concession), and discussed Sir Jon Cunliffe’s reform recommendations. Witnesses agreed the sector needs more investment, clearer planning at catchment level, and stronger, practical regulation; they sharply disagreed about whether public ownership is the best way to secure funds and outcomes. The debate focused on debt and dividend flows, the regulatory model (RCV/TotEx), and examples from France, the Netherlands, Scotland and Wales.

glossary.definition: The economic regulator for the water sector in England and Wales.
Regulatory Capital Value — an accounting measure regulators use to set allowed returns on water company assets.
The not-for-profit ownership model used by Welsh Water (Dŵr Cymru), where surplus is reinvested or returned to customers.
A contract where a public authority keeps ownership of assets but contracts a private operator to run services and bill users.
Total Expenditure — a regulatory concept that combines operational and capital spend for regulation and funding purposes.
A legal process to stabilise and re-organise a failing utility, with powers to transfer its assets or change ownership.

chapters.title: Why privatisation happened and what it changed
chapters.takeaway: Privatisation aimed to draw private finance and boost efficiency; it helped deliver major wastewater and drinking-water improvements but left funding and regulation choices that later caused problems.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’ll start in 1989: why was privatisation pursued and what problem was it meant to solve?

turns.speaker: Hugh Goldsmith
turns.text: The White Paper aimed to benefit customers: more efficiency, innovation and access to private finance. There was also a political aim of share ownership, but the practical goal was better services funded by private money.

turns.speaker: Dr David Lloyd Owen
turns.text: Privatisation itself wasn’t the issue; regulation was. Under the early regulator Ian Byatt there was focus on investment and maintenance. Later reviews shifted to keeping bills low and that squeezed maintenance.

turns.speaker: John Abraham
turns.text: Before 1989 water often lost out for public funding. Private ownership let big investments happen—especially secondary sewage treatment—and drove efficiency in design and construction.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So outcomes: has water quality and service improved overall since 1989?

turns.speaker: Hugh Goldsmith
turns.text: Yes: major improvements in waste water treatment and big falls in pollutants, driven in part by EU environmental rules; drinking water quality is among the world’s better systems.

chapters.title: Money, debt and the regulator’s role
chapters.takeaway: Regulatory accounting (RCV) and debt-financed investment led companies to rely heavily on borrowing; that, plus weak regulatory incentives for maintenance, created vulnerabilities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There’s a persistent claim that the industry was funded mainly by debt, not equity. How did that happen?

turns.speaker: Hugh Goldsmith
turns.text: Companies started debt-free at privatisation. The RCV model inflates asset values over time and made debt the natural way to fund investment; little fresh equity went in to build assets.

turns.speaker: Dr David Lloyd Owen
turns.text: Rating agencies and Ofwat set expectations. Companies took more debt; servicing it grew costly. Scotland’s public model shows similar debt levels can cost less because of cheaper borrowing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did regulatory choices prioritising low bills undermine maintenance?

turns.speaker: Dr David Lloyd Owen
turns.text: Yes. For 25 years operating and maintenance spend stayed flat despite new assets. That allowed assets to stagnate and left big repair backlogs.

turns.speaker: John Abraham
turns.text: Construction and CapEx delivery are good; the problem is operating and maintaining what we’ve built. England and Wales largely use the same in-house operators, so there's little competitive pressure on O&M.

chapters.title: Different ownership models abroad
chapters.takeaway: France, the Netherlands and other countries show many workable models — public ownership, municipal companies, concessions — but success depends on local capacity, finance and practical regulation.

turns.speaker: Dr Marine Colon
turns.text: In France local governments own assets and often sign concession contracts with private operators who bill users and are fined under contracts if they fail; local capacity matters more than ownership.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the pros and cons of that French concession model?

turns.speaker: Dr Marine Colon
turns.text: It allows local control and tailored contracts. But France has many tiny utilities that lack the expertise and finance to tackle large climate-driven investments; mergers and river-basin agencies help channel funds.

turns.speaker: Professor Klaas Schwartz
turns.text: The Dutch model uses private-law companies owned by municipalities or provinces, enshrined by law. They are autonomous but publicly owned, self-financing and trusted by consumers — but tariffs are rising because major reinvestment is needed.

turns.speaker: Hugh Goldsmith
turns.text: There’s no one-size-fits-all: Scandinavia has municipal systems and public banks to finance investment; Germany keeps assets public and outsources operations; Singapore mixes public ownership with private operators for specific projects.

turns.speaker: John Abraham
turns.text: In practice you can competitively tender operation and maintenance or concessions for catchments; many parts of the world do that well, but England and Wales largely don’t use that market for O&M.

chapters.title: Cunliffe’s reform agenda and the ownership debate
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses broadly back Cunliffe’s priorities — clear strategy, stronger regulation and funding — but sharply disagree on whether public ownership is the fastest, cheapest or fairest way to secure investment and better outcomes.

turns.speaker: David Henderson
turns.text: Sir Jon Cunliffe’s report is strong: you need Government strategy, a regulator that enforces it, and money (from bills or taxpayers). Ownership alone doesn’t determine outcomes.

turns.speaker: Professor David Saal
turns.text: I agree regulation needs reform and more local catchment planning. But that requires changing how Ofwat assesses costs; TotEx and the economic models must reflect local differences.

turns.speaker: Professor Ewan McGaughey
turns.text: Ownership matters a great deal. Since privatisation roughly £85bn has been returned to shareholders, and bondholders have taken large sums too. Public ownership lets the state avoid those extra returns and borrow cheaper.

turns.speaker: Professor David Hall
turns.text: The major omission from Cunliffe was public ownership options. Other countries put local accountable bodies in charge; here local authorities have almost no power and that damages accountability and trust.

turns.speaker: David Henderson
turns.text: Public ownership is an option but it would require taxpayers to back large sums. There are legal and market risks if the Government forcibly cancels contracts; funding still has to be found.

turns.speaker: Professor Ewan McGaughey
turns.text: Special administration can transfer assets without large compensation if shareholders have failed and statutory duties are neglected — that’s a practical route to remove badly performing private owners.

chapters.title: Public expectations, practical reforms and next steps
chapters.takeaway: The public overwhelmingly wants greater public control; practical reforms suggested include catchment-based planning, clearer regulation enforced by engineers, tighter dividend and debt rules, and exploring public acquisition where necessary.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Public opinion polls show strong support for public ownership. But practically, what changes would deliver better services now?

turns.speaker: Professor David Hall
turns.text: Start by restoring local responsibility and accountability: put planning and decision-making at catchment or regional level under public control, as other countries do.

turns.speaker: Professor David Saal
turns.text: Strengthen supervision: real engineers and auditors should assess assets and needs company-by-company or catchment-by-catchment instead of relying on opaque econometric models.

turns.speaker: John Abraham
turns.text: Introduce alternative delivery for operation and maintenance: ringfence catchments, competitively tender long-term O&M contracts, use instant penalties for breaches like PFIs do, and bring in global operators.

turns.speaker: Professor Ewan McGaughey
turns.text: Tighten rules on dividends and give Ofwat stronger, clearer licence powers; use special administration where owners have failed on pollution and leakage.

turns.speaker: David Henderson
turns.text: All models can work with the three ingredients Cunliffe sets out: clear national strategy, strong enforcement, and reliable funding. The Government must decide the trade-offs and act.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Committee will consider these trade-offs: public investment and ownership options, better local planning, and a regulatory model that focuses on real, practical asset needs.
